b: Rafael Manuel’s sumptuous debut exposes the ugly class divides lurking beneath the pristine fairways of a Manila golf resort.

It’s often said that the only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for wealthy, pompous men to spend an obscene amount of time perfecting their golf swing. It’s in this state of ease that the social elite accept the suffering needed to uphold their lavish lifestyle, and this charges the fascination of Filipino writer-director Rafael Manuel for his mesmerising debut, Filipiñana. It opens with a drone shot of Manila – shoulder-to-shoulder street markets and traffic resembling grandmaster- level Tetris. The Filipino capital finds itself in the grips of an inescapable heatwave, or so it would appear. But before you can say, “shit, it’s hot” – as one shuttle-bus guide puts it – we’re transported to the unnervingly pristine world of a golf resort.

Manuel empties out the full Wes Anderson box of crayons. From the pristine fairways to the textured marble staircases, everything feels bright and perfectly curated, but in a sickly, saccharine kind of way. Our window into this world comes through the eyes of new starter Isabel (Jorrybell Agoto), a diminutive 17-year-old from the Ilocos. On paper, her role as a tee girl situates her as a cog within an army of service workers, carrying out anything requested by the wealthy men. In reality, her outsider status means she hasn’t been indoctrinated yet. Why can’t she play on the greens too? If there’s a delicious cake that hasn’t been touched, surely she must be able to eat it?

Isabel’s story plays out in parallel to Clara’s (Carmen Castellanos), a Filipino expatriate living in New York and the niece of a flunky to Dr Palanca (Teroy Guzman), the course’s owner. The two girls unravel the world over the course of what feels like the longest summer day in the world, as if they’re pulling at the same string from different ends. Essential to the resort’s operations, the predominantly female workers are nevertheless treated as an ambient presence. They’re frequently framed in low shots, forcing us to share their worldview, one in which the wealthy are always looking down and they are always looking up.

Manuel doesn’t infantilise the club’s members as being oblivious to the bloodshed needed to uphold their reality. It’s just that their concerns are far more important. The gentrification of Isabel’s home, the Ilocos, is mere urinal chatter and the geopolitical concern of brain drain is only brought up by Clara’s uncle to convince her to return to the Philippines to take over his kingdom. These class dynamics invite comparisons to Bong Joon Ho’s Parasite, but things feel distinctly Filipino, particularly the film’s grasp of the country’s love affair with singing. Characters hum to themselves, the sounds stitch together scenes and create clever callbacks. Filipiñana is a methodical experience, luring you in with its luxury before snapping on you as the wickedness beneath it is uncovered.
